opus-5.5.text:
Real-time interactivity was really the defining constraint from the start, and it shaped almost every decision we made. With earlier world models, and with video generation models like Veo, you can afford to generate a whole clip at once. The model sees the full sequence, can refine it over many denoising steps, and nobody is waiting on the other side. Genie 3 doesn't have that luxury. The user presses a key, and they expect the world to respond right away, frame after frame, multiple times per second.

So the first big implication is that the model has to be autoregressive. It generates the world one frame at a time, conditioned on everything that has happened so far plus the action the user just took. You can't look ahead, because the future depends on what the user is going to do. That sounds simple, but it changes a lot. Errors can compound over time, so a lot of the work went into keeping the world stable and consistent over longer horizons, so that if you walk away from something and come back, it's still there and looks the way it did.

The second implication is the latency budget. Every frame has a fixed amount of time to be produced, so you're making trade-offs constantly between model size, quality, resolution, and how much compute you can spend per step. Some things that would improve quality in an offline setting just don't fit in the budget, so you have to be clever about where the compute goes, and you have to think about the model and the serving infrastructure together rather than treating them separately.

And third, interactivity means the model has to actually understand the consequences of actions, not just produce plausible-looking video. That pushed us toward thinking of it less as a video model and more as a world model, something that maintains an internal sense of the environment and how it evolves. Memory and consistency emerged as really central to that, and a lot of what makes Genie 3 feel different from earlier versions comes from that focus.

So in short, real time wasn't a feature we added at the end. It was the constraint everything else had to bend around.

r001.rationale: It says each frame is conditioned on everything that has happened so far and the latest action, but does not explain selecting relevant information from a potentially long history.

r002.rationale: It explains that users expect an immediate response to each action, frame after frame multiple times per second, and describes a fixed latency budget for producing each frame.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Real-time interactivity was really the north star for Genie 3, and it shaped almost every architectural decision we made.

With Genie 2, we could generate interactive environments, but the latency meant you'd take an action and wait. That's fine for a demo, but it's not a world you can inhabit. So for Genie 3, we set a hard constraint from the beginning: generate at around 24 frames per second, in real time, responding to a user's actions as they happen. Once you commit to that, a lot of options fall away.

The first big consequence is that the model has to be autoregressive at the frame level. You can't generate a whole clip and then let someone interact with it, because you don't know what they're going to do. Each frame has to be conditioned on everything that came before plus the action the user just took. That's a fundamentally different setup from most video generation models, which produce a fixed clip conditioned on a prompt.

The second consequence is memory. If you're generating frame by frame for minutes at a time, the model has to remember what it has already produced. If you turn around and look back, the room should still be the room you left. We spent a lot of effort on how the model attends to its own history efficiently, because you can't afford to recompute over the entire past every frame and still hit the latency target. Consistency over a long horizon emerged from that training, rather than from an explicit 3D representation like NeRFs or Gaussian splatting. We don't maintain a scene graph. The model learns to be consistent because it's trained to predict the next frame given a long interaction history.

The third thing was the action interface. We wanted both low-level controls, like moving and looking around, and what we call promptable world events, where you can type something and the world changes. Supporting both in real time meant designing the conditioning so that text and action inputs can be injected mid-stream without breaking the generation.

And honestly, a lot of it was engineering. Getting a large model to produce a 720p frame in a few tens of milliseconds, every time, with no hitches, took as much work on the inference side as on the modeling side.

The payoff is that it changes what the thing is for. A real-time, consistent, controllable world is something an agent can act in and learn from, not just something you watch. That was the motivation all along.

r001.rationale: It says each frame uses the prior interaction history and that the model attends to its history efficiently over long sessions, conveying attention to relevant information from that history.

r002.rationale: It explains that user actions are unknown in advance, so frames must be generated successively in real time at about 24 fps and respond as actions happen.

astra-6.text:
Real-time interactivity makes latency a central constraint. You can’t generate a whole video, wait for it to finish, and then let the user decide what to do. The user takes an action, the world responds, and that response informs their next action.

So the architecture has to support generating the world as you go, conditioned on the user’s actions and what has already happened. And there are two challenges that have to be solved together: producing the next frames quickly enough to feel responsive, and maintaining enough consistency that it feels like you’re interacting with a persistent world.

That changes how you think about quality, too. It’s not just whether an individual frame looks good. It’s whether the world responds coherently when you change direction or try something unexpected. The goal is to keep that action-and-response loop working while preserving the richness of the environment.

r001.rationale: The response mentions conditioning generation on user actions and what has already happened, but it does not explain selecting relevant information from a potentially long history of prior events.

r002.rationale: It says the next frames must be produced quickly enough to feel responsive so the user can act, receive a response, and act again.

sol-6.1.text:
Real-time interactivity makes latency a central design constraint. You can’t generate an entire video, wait for it to finish, and then let the user decide what to do. The model has to take an action, produce the next part of the world quickly, and be ready for another action.

So the architecture needs to support that continuous loop: observe the current state, incorporate the user’s input, and generate what happens next. And it has to do that while maintaining consistency. If you turn around or revisit somewhere, you want it to feel like you’re still in the same world.

That creates a balance between generation quality, speed, and memory. A beautiful individual frame isn’t sufficient—the experience has to respond to you, and the sequence of responses has to make sense. That interaction loop is really what drives the design.

r001.rationale: The response mentions consistency and revisiting places, but does not explain selecting relevant information from a long history of prior events to generate each next frame.

r002.rationale: It says the model must quickly produce the next part of the world and be ready for another action, explicitly making low latency central to real-time interactivity.
